html:
This bar covers the independent states of South Asia after British rule ended: India and Pakistan from 1947, Sri Lanka (then Ceylon) from 1948, and Bangladesh from 1971. Together they hold about a quarter of the world's people.

The Partition of 1947 split British India into a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan, in two pieces a thousand miles apart. It came with mass killing and the flight of millions. The new states fought over Kashmir within months, and the Kashmir conflict has run ever since.

Their paths then split:

  • India under Nehru became a federal, secular democracy under its 1950 Constitution. Elections have held except for Indira Gandhi's Emergency of 1975 to 1977. The Green Revolution ended mass famine, and reforms from 1991 brought fast growth.
  • Pakistan lost its founder, Jinnah, in 1948 and swung between civilian and military rule.
  • Bangladesh was East Pakistan until the Liberation War of 1971, which India joined and which sent about ten million refugees across the border.
  • Sri Lanka had an early start with universal suffrage, then a long civil war from 1983 to 2009 between the state and Tamil separatists.

India and Pakistan both tested nuclear weapons in 1998. The region shares rivers, cricket, film and a long history, and is still one of the least economically connected regions in the world.
sum: This bar covers the independent states of South Asia after British rule ended: India and Pakistan from 1947, Sri Lanka (then Ceylon) from 1948, and Bangladesh from 1971. Together they hold about a quarter of the world's people.
